q: do fungi communicate with each other
a: Fungi communicate with each other and with plants through an underground network called the mycorrhizal network, often referred to as the Wood Wide Web. The network is made of thread-like structures called hyphae that form mycelium, which can spread for miles underground. Through this network, fungi can send chemical signals, transfer nutrients, and even share information about threats like pests or drought. When a plant is attacked by insects, it can release chemical signals through the fungal network that warn neighboring plants to activate their defense mechanisms. Fungi also use electrical impulses, similar to nerve signals in animals, to communicate across their mycelial networks. Research by Professor Andrew Adamatzky at the University of the West of England has shown that fungi generate rhythmic electrical spikes that resemble language, with different patterns of electrical activity corresponding to different stimuli. These signals travel through the mycelium at rates comparable to nerve conduction in animals. The network also allows trees to share resources: older trees can send carbon and nutrients through the fungal network to younger saplings, helping them survive. About 90% of all land plants are connected through these fungal networks, making them one of the most extensive and ancient communication systems on Earth.
